name: Daria Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a detergent-bottle labeller and still call the setter when the reel wanders across the fill mark. I moved from the plant canteen two years ago, so I am a junior operator and still learning; I finished secondary school. The pay is low for this job, and I like getting one clean batch before the next shift.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and what do you use on your phone?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Mateo works part-time grocery shifts, and our grown children live in their own homes. We rent, have saved less than a month of expenses and have few similar factory jobs nearby. I am fifty-eight, with retirement somewhere ahead but no clear sum yet; I use an AI phone tool now and then after a colleague showed me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the detergent line that an AI slowdown leaves the bottles and labels where they are. I am still learning how to catch a crooked roll before a whole batch is marked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is my second year on the labeller after years in the plant canteen, so I am the junior one on a low wage. Mateo has part-time grocery shifts, our children are grown, and less than a month is saved against rent and household bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid labeller shift and ask the setter to check my first roll on changeover. If a Saturday shift is offered, I would put a fresh part of that wage into a reserve after rent; I would keep using the same AI phone tool now and then to read unclear instructions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about money even in a quiet AI world. A broken fridge could use everything we have saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What goes wrong on the labeller?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the reel wanders, the label covers the fill mark and boxes have to be reopened. I still call the setter before adjusting the guide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did you start using the phone tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A younger operator showed me last year how to ask it what a fault message means. I check the answer against the printed manual before touching the machine.

say: I would say **bottle labels** still need careful checks.
I would ask the **setter** about the first roll.
think: My **junior wage** and Mateo’s part-time pay barely cover bills.
Less than **one month saved** makes an ordinary repair difficult.
do: Keep **paid labeller shifts** and ask for first-roll checks.
Use the **existing AI phone tool** only with manual checks.
Save fresh **offered Saturday wages** after rent.
feel: **Anxious** about baseline bills and a tiny reserve.
S0.quote: A broken fridge could use everything we have saved.
fieldNote: Daria’s **secondary schooling** and recent move from the canteen make her a junior operator at fifty-eight.
Her **fragile household cash** justifies anxiety even when AI adds little; savings require an offered paid shift.

steps.text: Keep labeller shifts and ask setter to check first roll
Save fresh offered Saturday wages after rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say scheduling software may change office work first, while robot bottle handling reaches our line more slowly. Before they remove a pair of hands, I want the plant to show us the paid roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The camera might take label checks I am still learning, and I could be one of the first juniors to lose hours. Mateo’s grocery pay cannot cover our bills alone, and nearby packaging jobs are scarce.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the next two rotas and watch an experienced colleague test the new camera. If the plant offers a paid guarded place with a qualified setter, I would learn its reject screen on stopped bottles; if my own hours fall, I would search posted reachable packaging work only where pay after travel covers rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious, though I can ask for a demonstration and look for work. I need a paid shift more than a new screen to admire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start the camera lesson tomorrow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a real paid practice place opens and the reject gate is isolated. A demonstration from across the aisle would not let me run it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I need to price it with Mateo before I count on leaving work. Right now a cut to either wage would reach our rent quickly.

say: I would ask for a **written paid roster** before a camera reduces staff.
I would separate **office scheduling** from later robot handling.
think: My **junior label checks** may disappear as the camera takes more of the routine work.
Mateo’s **grocery shifts** cannot cover our bills without my wage.
do: Request **two rotas** and watch a colleague test the camera.
Learn **new reject controls** only in offered paid guarded practice.
Search after **hour cuts** for posted reachable packaging work at bill-covering net pay.
feel: **Anxious** about a likely cut to her own paid week.
S1.quote: I need a paid shift more than a new screen to admire.
fieldNote: Her **steady adaptability** follows a colleague’s proven camera use before new hands-on practice.
Learning requires an **offered safe paid place**; outside work needs real cuts, local postings and net wages after travel.

steps.text: Request two written rotas and observe proven camera use
Learn new reject controls only in offered paid guarded practice
Search after cuts for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay packaging work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AGI could arrive by 2028 when I am sixty, while capable bottle robots follow around 2031 when I am sixty-three. Ordering changes first; the hands-on labelling hours disappear later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most junior labeller shifts to go once the robots can feed and inspect bottles. Mateo’s grocery hours and our sub-month reserve cannot carry rent through a long loss; I would lie awake over the next payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cancel our planned visit to the grown children and ask for written staffing dates. If my paid shift ends, I would apply only for posted reachable work with net pay after travel covering our bills; if no adequate role appears, I would ask the landlord about time to pay and the children about temporary help only if they can afford it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed by a likely large loss of household income. My grown children have their own rent, so I cannot make them our pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you apply for a care job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if an actual paid local vacancy is posted and the shifts fit my health. I would not call a course enquiry a job offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have no figures that promise enough income then. I would check the accounts and keep safe paid work if the household still needs it.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AGI** from 2031 bottle robots.
I would ask for **written staffing dates** before a physical cut.
think: I expect **most labeller shifts** to go after capable robots arrive.
Our **sub-month reserve** and part-time grocery pay cannot replace my wage.
do: Cancel **family visit** and request staffing dates.
Apply after **lost shifts** only for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work.
Ask **landlord about timing** if no adequate job; request temporary family help only if the children can afford it.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major income loss and sleepless rent worry.
S2.quote: My grown children have their own rent, so I cannot make them our pension.
fieldNote: Her **age sixty-three** at physical robot arrival makes a funded retirement uncertain.
The search and support requests retain **real conditions**: a posted vacancy, net pay after travel, health fit and children able to help.

steps.text: Cancel family visit and request written staffing dates
Apply after lost shifts for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay job
Ask landlord about payment timing if no adequate job appears
Ask children for temporary help only if affordable and no adequate job appears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AGI in 2031 finds me sixty-three, and capable robots around 2034 find me sixty-six. Five years gives the plant time to offer paid instruction, not just tell older juniors to wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands are slower on the labeller than some younger operators, but I can learn a routine if someone shows it on a stopped machine. I cannot pay tuition or lose wages for a certificate with no local post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the labeller shift and add any fresh spare pay from full months to savings. If the plant offers a funded quality-check course on paid time with an actual safe practical place and a posted reachable job at bill-covering net pay, I would enrol and apply after qualifying; if no place opens, I would search posted local operator work after hours fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious, with time to ask who pays for the course. A certificate does not buy groceries unless somebody hires me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would safe practice include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The setter would stop the conveyor and let me gauge a label and reject gate before restart. I would need an offered paid slot, not a video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire instead of taking a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if actual retirement income and Mateo’s wages cover our rent and food. I cannot decide that from a birthday.

say: I would ask for **paid practical instruction** before 2034 robots.
I would name **real local jobs** before a course.
think: My **low wages** leave no room for unpaid study while rent and food still come due.
A **quality certificate** matters only with bill-covering work.
do: Keep **labeller shifts** and save fresh full-month surplus.
Enrol in **funded paid quality training** only with offered safe place and adequate posted job.
Apply after **qualification** for the reachable quality role.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to test actual terms.
S3.quote: A certificate does not buy groceries unless somebody hires me.
fieldNote: She would accept **practical paid learning** despite a preference for familiar work.
The application requires **accepted funded safe training**, a posted reachable vacancy and net wages sufficient for rent and food.

steps.text: Save fresh full-month surplus while keeping labeller shifts
Enrol if funded paid safe quality place and adequate posted job exist
Apply after qualification for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay quality job
Search posted local operator jobs after cuts if no course place opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the plant that thinking AGI in 2036 arrives when I am sixty-eight, and capable robots around 2039 when I am seventy-one. Ten years is enough to price retirement honestly and keep safe work available for people who need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children will have their own households, but I do not know what my pension or Mateo’s wage will be. Less than a month saved today means I cannot treat sixty-eight as a guaranteed exit from paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep the labeller shift and save fresh full-month surplus after rent. I would request pension figures and a rent-and-food budget with Mateo; in the first year after 2036, if still employed because income requires it, I would check actual rosters and apply after sustained cuts only for posted reachable safe work with enough net pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about our present money, even with a decade before the robots. A long clock does not fill the savings account this winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you stop before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the actual pension figures and Mateo’s pay cover rent, food and a repair buffer. I would not leave a safe paid shift on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn a new system then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I am still working and offered paid safe instruction, I would listen. I cannot promise the plant will still have a junior place in ten years.

say: I would ask for **honest retirement figures** before 2036.
I would separate **2036 AGI** from 2039 physical robots.
think: Our **rent and low savings** still matter today.
A future **pension amount** is unknown, so work may remain necessary.
do: Keep **2026 labeller shifts** and save fresh surplus after rent.
Request **pension figures** and review household costs with Mateo.
Apply after **post-2036 cuts** only if still employed and net pay covers bills.
feel: **Anxious** about present money despite a distant robot date.
S4.quote: A long clock does not fill the savings account this winter.
fieldNote: Her **2026 paid work** is current; post-2036 job search requires continued employment and actual cuts.
Retirement remains **conditional on verified income**, not an assumed pension age or benefit amount.

steps.text: Save fresh full-month surplus while keeping labeller shifts

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could remove junior labeller work when I am sixty-three and still need rent money. Written staffing dates, paid safe learning and posted reachable jobs with bill-covering net pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what a late new starter is meant to do with an unpaid course. I can still work, but I cannot buy a promise instead of groceries.

headlineQuote: I can still work, but I cannot buy a promise instead of groceries.
portrait: **Daria**, 58, is a junior detergent-line operator after a late move from the canteen, with secondary schooling and skills still developing.
Her **part-time grocery partner**, grown children, rent, low pay, sub-month savings and few local plants make lost shifts serious.
She uses **AI occasionally** for fault explanations, follows proven colleagues and needs offered paid safe practice for new controls.
Fast robots threaten **labeller hours** at sixty-three; longer warning permits conditional quality training and an income-based retirement review.
biggestWorry: **Fast physical robots** could remove junior labeller shifts around 2031 before she has enough saved to stop working.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing dates**, funded safe practical learning and posted reachable work at bill-covering net pay would help.
